Excerpt (ONLY factual source):
[textbook.md line 651~657]

The tensor product is a way of putting vector spaces together to form larger vector spaces.
This construction is crucial to understanding the quantum mechanics of multiparticle systems.
The following discussion is a little abstract, and may be difficult to follow if you're not already familiar with the tensor product, so feel free to skip ahead now and revisit later when you come to the discussion of tensor products in quantum mechanics.

Suppose $V$ and $W$ are vector spaces of dimension $m$ and $n$ respectively.
For convenience we also suppose that $V$ and $W$ are Hilbert spaces.
Then $V \otimes W$ (read '$V$ tensor $W$') is an $m n$ dimensional vector space.
---
[textbook.md line 702~705]

The elements of $V \otimes W$ are linear combinations of 'tensor products' $|v\rangle \otimes|w\rangle$ of elements $|v\rangle$ of $V$ and $|w\rangle$ of $W$.
In particular, if $|i\rangle$ and $|j\rangle$ are orthonormal bases for the spaces $V$ and $W$ then $|i\rangle \otimes|j\rangle$ is a basis for $V \otimes W$.
We often use the abbreviated notations $|v\rangle|w\rangle,|v, w\rangle$ or even $|v w\rangle$ for the tensor product
$|v\rangle \otimes|w\rangle$.
<<<END_ITEM>>>

<<<ITEM id="i57" kind="admonition" type="theorem">
Blueprint content:
basic properties of tensor product

Excerpt (ONLY factual source):
[textbook.md line 708~733]

By definition the tensor product satisfies the following basic properties:
(1) For an arbitrary scalar $z$ and elements $|v\rangle$ of $V$ and $|w\rangle$ of $W$,

$$
\begin{equation*}
z(|v\rangle \otimes|w\rangle)=(z|v\rangle) \otimes|w\rangle=|v\rangle \otimes(z|w\rangle) \tag{2.42}
\end{equation*}
$$

(2) For arbitrary $\left|v_{1}\right\rangle$ and $\left|v_{2}\right\rangle$ in $V$ and $|w\rangle$ in $W$,

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left(\left|v_{1}\right\rangle+\left|v_{2}\right\rangle\right) \otimes|w\rangle=\left|v_{1}\right\rangle \otimes|w\rangle+\left|v_{2}\right\rangle \otimes|w\rangle .
\tag{2.43}
\end{equation*}
$$

(3) For arbitrary $|v\rangle$ in $V$ and $\left|w_{1}\right\rangle$ and $\left|w_{2}\right\rangle$ in $W$,

$$
\begin{equation*}
|v\rangle \otimes\left(\left|w_{1}\right\rangle+\left|w_{2}\right\rangle\right)=|v\rangle \otimes\left|w_{1}\right\rangle+|v\rangle \otimes\left|w_{2}\right\rangle .
\tag{2.44}
\end{equation*}
$$
<<<END_ITEM>>>

<<<ITEM id="i58" kind="admonition" type="definition">
Blueprint content:
linear operators in tensor products

Excerpt (ONLY factual source):
[textbook.md line 735~757]

What sorts of linear operators act on the space $V \otimes W$ ?
Suppose $|v\rangle$ and $|w\rangle$ are vectors in $V$ and $W$, and $A$ and $B$ are linear operators on $V$ and $W$, respectively.
Then we can define a linear operator $A \otimes B$ on $V \otimes W$ by the equation

$$
\begin{equation*}
(A \otimes B)(|v\rangle \otimes|w\rangle) \equiv A|v\rangle \otimes B|w\rangle .
\tag{2.45}
\end{equation*}
$$

The definition of $A \otimes B$ is then extended to all elements of $V \otimes W$ in the natural way to ensure linearity of $A \otimes B$, that is,

$$
\begin{equation*}
(A \otimes B)\left(\sum_{i} a_{i}\left|v_{i}\right\rangle \otimes\left|w_{i}\right\rangle\right) \equiv \sum_{i} a_{i} A\left|v_{i}\right\rangle \otimes B\left|w_{i}\right\rangle .
\tag{2.46}
\end{equation*}
$$

It can be shown that $A \otimes B$ defined in this way is a well-defined linear operator on $V \otimes W$.
This notion of the tensor product of two operators extends in the obvious way to the case where $A: V \rightarrow V^{\prime}$ and $B: W \rightarrow W^{\prime}$ map between different vector spaces.
Indeed, an arbitrary linear operator $C$ mapping $V \otimes W$ to $V^{\prime} \otimes W^{\prime}$ can be represented as a linear combination of tensor products of operators mapping $V$ to $V^{\prime}$ and $W$ to $W^{\prime}$,
<<<END_ITEM>>>

Theorem 2.3: (Polar decomposition) Let $A$ be a linear operator on a vector space $V$.
Then there exists unitary $U$ and positive operators $J$ and $K$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
A=U J=K U, \tag{2.79}
\end{equation*}
$$

Moreover, if $A$ is invertible then $U$ is unique.

"'!!! definition "Definition 2.1.12 : Inner Product and Inner Product Space"
    An inner product is a function that takes two vectors $|v'"\\rangle"'$ and $|w'"\\rangle"'$ from a vector space and produces a complex number.
    For convenience, we write it as $(|v'"\\rangle,|w\\rangle)"'$, or in quantum notation as $'"\\langle v \\mid w\\rangle"'$.
    The notation $'"\\langle v|"'$ denotes the dual vector to $|v'"\\rangle"'$; it is the linear operator from $V$ to $'"\\mathbf{C}"'$ defined by

    $$
    '"\\langle v|(|w\\rangle) \\equiv \\langle v \\mid w\\rangle \\equiv (|v\\rangle,|w\\rangle).
    "'$$

    A function $('"\\cdot,\\cdot)"'$ from $V '"\\times V"'$ to $'"\\mathbf{C}"'$ is an inner product if:

    1. $('"\\cdot,\\cdot)"'$ is linear in the second argument,

    $$
    '"\\begin{equation*}
    (|v\\rangle, \\sum_{i} \\lambda_{i}|w_{i}\\rangle)=\\sum_{i} \\lambda_{i}(|v\\rangle,|w_{i}\\rangle) .
    \\tag{2.13}
    \\end{equation*}
    "'$$

    2. $(|v'"\\rangle,|w\\rangle)=(|w\\rangle,|v\\rangle)"'^{*}$.

    3. $(|v'"\\rangle,|v\\rangle)\\geq 0"'$ with equality iff $|v'"\\rangle=0"'$.

    For example, $'"\\mathbf{C}"'^{n}$ has the inner product

    $$
    '"\\left((y_{1},\\ldots,y_{n}),(z_{1},\\ldots,z_{n})\\right) \\equiv \\sum_{i} y_{i}"'^{*} z_{i}='"\\left[y_{1}"'^{*} '"\\ldots y_{n}"'^{*}'"\\right]\\left[\\begin{array}{c}
    z_{1} \\\\
    \\vdots \\\\
    z_{n}
    \\end{array}\\right]
    \\tag{2.14}
    "'$$

    We call a vector space equipped with an inner product an inner product space.
EOF

cat > backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/stage/i17.document <<'"'EOF'
"'!!! definition "Definition 2.1.13 : Dual Vector"
    The standard quantum mechanical notation for the inner product $(|v'"\\rangle,|w\\rangle)"'$ is $'"\\langle v \\mid w\\rangle"'$.
    Here $'"\\langle v|"'$ is the dual vector to $|v'"\\rangle"'$ and is a linear operator from the inner product space $V$ to the complex numbers, with

    $$
    '"\\langle v|(|w\\rangle) \\equiv \\langle v \\mid w\\rangle \\equiv (|v\\rangle,|w\\rangle).

    We will see shortly that the matrix representation of dual vectors is a row vector.

    We also see that the dual vector $'"\\langle v|"'$ has a row-vector interpretation whose components are complex conjugates of those of the column representation of $|v'"\\rangle"'$.

"'!!! definition "Definition 2.1.17 : Orthogonal, Orthonormal, Norm, Normalized"
    Vectors $|w'"\\rangle"'$ and $|v'"\\rangle"'$ are orthogonal if their inner product is zero.
    For example, $|w'"\\rangle=(1,0)"'$ and $|v'"\\rangle=(0,1)"'$ are orthogonal with respect to the inner product defined by (2.14).

    The norm of $|v'"\\rangle"'$ is

    $$
    '"\\begin{equation*}
    \\||v\\rangle \\| \\equiv \\sqrt{\\langle v \\mid v\\rangle} .
    \\tag{2.16}
    \\end{equation*}
    "'$$

    A unit vector is a vector $|v'"\\rangle"'$ such that $'"\\||v\\rangle \\|=1"'$.
    Equivalently, $|v'"\\rangle"'$ is normalized if $'"\\||v\\rangle \\|=1"'$.
    Normalizing a vector is done by dividing by its norm: $|v'"\\rangle / \\||v\\rangle \\|"'$ is the normalized form of non-zero $|v'"\\rangle"'$.

    A set $|i'"\\rangle"'$ is orthonormal if each vector is unit and distinct vectors are orthogonal, so that $'"\\langle i\\mid j\\rangle=\\delta_{ij}"'$.
EOF

cat > backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/stage/i22.document <<'"'EOF'
"'!!! theorem "Theorem 2.1.18 : Gram-Schmidt Procedure"
    There is a useful method, the Gram-Schmidt procedure, to produce an orthonormal basis $|v_{1}'"\\rangle,\\ldots,|v_{d}\\rangle"'$ for a vector space $V$.
    Define

    $$
    |v_{1}'"\\rangle \\equiv |w_{1}\\rangle / \\| |w_{1}\\rangle \\|,
    "'$$

    and for $1'"\\le k \\le d-1"'$ define inductively

    $$
    '"\\begin{equation*}
    |v_{k+1}\\rangle \\equiv \\frac{|w_{k+1}\\rangle-\\sum_{i=1}"'^{k}'"\\langle v_{i} \\mid w_{k+1}\\rangle|v_{i}\\rangle}{\\| |w_{k+1}\\rangle-\\sum_{i=1}"'^{k}'"\\langle v_{i} \\mid w_{k+1}\\rangle|v_{i}\\rangle \\|} . \\tag{2.17}
    \\end{equation*}
    "'$$

    It is not difficult to verify that the vectors $|v_{1}'"\\rangle,\\ldots,|v_{d}\\rangle"'$ form an orthonormal basis.
    Thus any finite dimensional vector space of dimension $d$ has an orthonormal basis.

    Exercise 2.8: Prove that the Gram-Schmidt procedure produces an orthonormal basis for $V$.

"'!!! theorem "Theorem 2.1.19 : Inner Product in Matrix Form"
    With orthonormal basis vectors $|i'"\\rangle"'$, let

    $$
    |w'"\\rangle=\\sum_{i} w_{i}|i\\rangle, \\quad |v\\rangle=\\sum_{j} v_{j}|j\\rangle.
    "'$$

    Since $'"\\langle i\\mid j\\rangle=\\delta_{ij}"'$,

    $$
    '"\\begin{align*}
    \\langle v \\mid w\\rangle &=(\\sum_{i} v_{i}|i\\rangle, \\sum_{j} w_{j}|j\\rangle)=\\sum_{ij} v_{i}"'^{*} w_{j}'"\\delta_{ij}=\\sum_{i} v_{i}"'^{*}w_{i} '"\\tag{2.18} \\\\
    &=[v_{1}"'^{*}'"\\ldots v_{n}"'^{*}]'"\\left[\\begin{array}{c}
    w_{1} \\\\
    \\vdots \\\\
    w_{n}
    \\end{array}\\right] . \\tag{2.19}
    \\end{align*}
    "'$$

    That is, the inner product of two vectors is the vector inner product between two matrix representations, provided the same orthonormal basis.

"'!!! definition "Definition 2.1.20 : Outer Product"
    Suppose $|v'"\\rangle"'$ is in an inner product space $V$ and $|w'"\\rangle"'$ is in an inner product space $W$.
    Define

    $$
    '"\\begin{equation*}
    (|w\\rangle\\langle v|)(|v'\\rangle) \\equiv |w\\rangle\\langle v\\mid v'\\rangle=\\langle v\\mid v'\\rangle|w\\rangle . \\tag{2.20}
    \\end{equation*}
    "'$$

    This is the outer product representation, and by definition the two possible interpretations of $|w'"\\rangle\\langle v\\mid v'\\rangle"'$ coincide.

    Linear combinations are defined in the obvious way: by definition

    $$
    '"\\sum_{i} a_{i}|w_{i}\\rangle\\langle v_{i}|
    "'$$

    '"\\sum_{i} a_{i}|w_{i}\\rangle\\langle v_{i}\\mid v'\\rangle.

cat > backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/stage/i26.document <<'"'EOF'
"'!!! theorem "Theorem 2.1.21 : Completeness Relation"
    For any orthonormal basis $|i'"\\rangle"'$ of $V$, any vector $|v'"\\rangle"'$ can be written $|v'"\\rangle=\\sum_{i} v_{i}|i\\rangle"'$, where $'"\\langle i\\mid v\\rangle=v_{i}"'$.
    Hence

    $$
    '"\\begin{equation*}
    \\left(\\sum_{i}|i\\rangle\\langle i|\\right)|v\\rangle=\\sum_{i}|i\\rangle\\langle i\\mid v\\rangle=\\sum_{i} v_{i}|i\\rangle=|v\\rangle. \\tag{2.21}
    \\end{equation*}
    "'$$

    Since this is true for all $|v'"\\rangle"'$,

    $$
    '"\\begin{equation*}
    \\sum_{i}|i\\rangle\\langle i|=I . \\tag{2.22}
    \\end{equation*}
    "'$$

    This is the completeness relation.

"'!!! definition "Definition 2.1.24 : Eigenvector, Eigenvalue, Characteristic Function, Eigenspace"
    An eigenvector of a linear operator $A$ on a vector space is a non-zero vector $|v'"\\rangle"'$ such that

    $$
    A|v'"\\rangle = v|v\\rangle,
    "'$$

    where $v$ is the eigenvalue.
    We use the notation $v$ both as a label for the eigenvector and for the eigenvalue.

    The characteristic function is

    $$
    c('"\\lambda) \\equiv \\operatorname{det}|A-\\lambda I|,
    "'$$

    and depends only on $A$, not on the specific matrix representation.
    Solutions of $c('"\\lambda)=0"'$ are the eigenvalues of $A$.
    By the fundamental theorem of algebra every operator has at least one eigenvalue and a corresponding eigenvector.

    The eigenspace corresponding to eigenvalue $v$ is the set of vectors with eigenvalue $v$.
    It is a vector subspace of the vector space on which $A$ acts.
EOF

cat > backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/stage/i31.document <<'"'EOF'
"'!!! definition "Definition 2.1.25 : Diagonal Representation and Orthonormal Decomposition"
    A diagonal representation for operator $A$ on a vector space $V$ is

    $$
    A='"\\sum_{i} \\lambda_{i}|i\\rangle\\langle i|,
    "'$$

    where the vectors $|i'"\\rangle"'$ form an orthonormal set of eigenvectors for $A$ with eigenvalues $'"\\lambda_i"'$.
    An operator is diagonalizable if it has a diagonal representation.

    As an example, Pauli $Z$ is

    $$
    Z='"\\left[\\begin{array}{rr}
    1 & 0 \\\\
    0 & -1
    \\end{array}\\right]=|0\\rangle\\langle 0|-|1\\rangle\\langle 1|,
    "'$$

    where the matrix representation is with respect to orthonormal vectors $|0'"\\rangle"'$ and $|1'"\\rangle"'$.
    Diagonal representations are sometimes also called orthonormal decompositions.

cat > backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/stage/i42.document <<'"'EOF'
"'!!! theorem "Theorem 2.1.35 : Spectral Theorem"
    The spectral decomposition is an extremely useful representation theorem for normal operators.

    Any normal operator $M$ on a vector space $V$ is diagonal with respect to some orthonormal basis for $V$.
    Conversely, any diagonalizable operator is normal.

    We prove the forward implication by induction on the dimension $d$ of $V$.
    Let $'"\\lambda"'$ be an eigenvalue of $M$, $P$ the projector onto the $'"\\lambda"'$ eigenspace, and $Q$ the projector onto its orthogonal complement.
    Then

    $$
    M=(P+Q) M(P+Q)=P M P+Q M P+ P M Q+Q M Q
    $$

    with $P M P='"\\lambda P"'$ and $Q M P=0$, $P M Q=0$.
    Thus $M=P M P+Q M Q$.

    Then $Q M Q$ is normal and, by induction, diagonal in some orthonormal basis of $Q$.
    Since $P M P$ is already diagonal in an orthonormal basis of $P$, we get an orthonormal basis of $V$ that diagonalizes $M$:

    $$
    M='"\\sum_{i} \\lambda_{i}|i\\rangle\\langle i|.
    "'$$

    In projector form, $M='"\\sum_{i} \\lambda_{i} P_{i}"'$, with orthonormality $P_{i}P_{j}='"\\delta_{ij}P_{i}"'$ and completeness $'"\\sum_i P_i=I"'$.
EOF

cat > backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/stage/i56.document <<'EOF'
"'!!! definition "Definition 2.1.48 : Tensor Products"
    The tensor product combines vector spaces into larger ones.
    Suppose $V$ and $W$ are vector spaces of dimensions $m$ and $n$.
    Then $V '"\\otimes W"'$ is an $mn$-dimensional vector space.

    The elements of $V '"\\otimes W"'$ are linear combinations of tensor products $|v'"\\rangle \\otimes |w\\rangle"'$.
    If $|i'"\\rangle"'$ and $|j'"\\rangle"'$ are orthonormal bases for $V$ and $W$, then $|i'"\\rangle \\otimes |j\\rangle"'$ is a basis for $V '"\\otimes W"'$.

    We often abbreviate $|v'"\\rangle \\otimes|w\\rangle"'$ as $|v'"\\rangle|w\\rangle"'$, $|v,w'"\\rangle"'$, or $|vw'"\\rangle"'$.
EOF

cat > backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/stage/i57.document <<'"'EOF'
"'!!! theorem "Theorem 2.1.49 : Basic Properties of Tensor Product"
    For scalar $z$ and vectors $|v'"\\rangle\\in V"'$, $|w'"\\rangle\\in W"'$:

    $$
    '"\\begin{equation*}
    z(|v\\rangle \\otimes|w\\rangle)=(z|v\\rangle) \\otimes|w\\rangle=|v\\rangle \\otimes(z|w\\rangle). \\tag{2.42}
    \\end{equation*}
    "'$$

    For $|v_1'"\\rangle,|v_2\\rangle\\in V"'$ and $|w'"\\rangle\\in W"'$:

    $$
    '"\\begin{equation*}
    (|v_1\\rangle+|v_2\\rangle)\\otimes|w\\rangle=|v_1\\rangle\\otimes|w\\rangle+|v_2\\rangle\\otimes|w\\rangle. \\tag{2.43}
    \\end{equation*}
    "'$$

    For $|v'"\\rangle\\in V"'$ and $|w_1'"\\rangle,|w_2\\rangle\\in W"'$:

    $$
    '"\\begin{equation*}
    |v\\rangle\\otimes(|w_1\\rangle+|w_2\\rangle)=|v\\rangle\\otimes|w_1\\rangle+|v\\rangle\\otimes|w_2\\rangle. \\tag{2.44}
    \\end{equation*}
    "'$$
EOF

cat > backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/stage/i58.document <<'"'EOF'
"'!!! definition "Definition 2.1.50 : Tensor Product of Linear Operators"
    Suppose $|v'"\\rangle"'$ and $|w'"\\rangle"'$ are vectors in $V$ and $W$, and $A,B$ are linear operators on $V$ and $W$.
    The linear operator $A'"\\otimes B"'$ on $V'"\\otimes W"'$ is defined by

    $$
    '"\\begin{equation*}
    (A\\otimes B)(|v\\rangle\\otimes|w\\rangle)\\equiv A|v\\rangle\\otimes B|w\\rangle. \\tag{2.45}
    \\end{equation*}
    "'$$

    and extended linearly:

    $$
    '"\\begin{equation*}
    (A\\otimes B)\\left(\\sum_{i} a_{i}|v_{i}\\rangle\\otimes|w_{i}\\rangle\\right) \\equiv \\sum_{i} a_{i} A|v_{i}\\rangle \\otimes B|w_{i}\\rangle. \\tag{2.46}
    \\end{equation*}
    "'$$

    It can be shown that this is a well-defined linear operator.
    The notion extends when $A:V'"\\to V'"'$ and $B:W'"\\to W'"'$.
EOF

cat > backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/stage/i59.document <<'"'EOF'

    The inner products on $V$ and $W$ give a natural inner product on $V'"\\otimes W"'$ by

"'!!! definition "Definition 2.1.52 : Kronecker Product"
    A linear operator tensor product has the matrix representation known as the Kronecker product.
    Suppose $A$ is $m'"\\times n"'$ and $B$ is $p'"\\times q"'$. Then

    $$
    A'"\\otimes B \\equiv \\overbrace{\\left[\\begin{array}{cccc}
    A_{11} B & A_{12} B & \\ldots & A_{1 n} B \\\\

cat > backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/stage/i70.document <<'"'EOF'
"'!!! theorem "Theorem 2.1.61 : Properties of Trace"
    The trace is cyclic and linear:

    $$
    '"\\operatorname{tr}(A B)=\\operatorname{tr}(B A),
    "'$$

    $$
    '"\\operatorname{tr}(A+B)= \\operatorname{tr}(A)+\\operatorname{tr}(B), \\quad \\operatorname{tr}(z A)=z \\operatorname{tr}(A),
    "'$$

    where $A,B$ are arbitrary matrices and $z$ is complex.
    From cyclicity, trace is invariant under unitary similarity: $
    '"\\operatorname{tr}(U A U"'^{'"\\dagger})=\\operatorname{tr}(A)"'$.

    In light of this, we define the trace of an operator as the trace of any matrix representation of it.
EOF

"'!!! definition "Definition 2.1.66 : Commutator"

    [A, B] \\equiv A B-B A . \\tag{2.66}

cat > backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/stage/i77.document <<'"'EOF'

    \\end{equation*}
    "'$$

    We say $A$ anti-commutes with $B$ if $'"\\{A,B\\}=0"'$.
